The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p50 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:49:02Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:49:27Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:43:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T03:50:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 7 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 1 minute 44 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:51:07Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 1.5% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - stretches as long before it began averaged as high on their own.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.5"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p50 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 26.616666666666667 ms {series_before} before it began, 189.57142857142858 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 191 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:

  - [T2] 2026-11-11T03:49:27Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up

  - [T4] 2026-11-11T03:49:33Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 03:49:02 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T03:49:37Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T03:49:38Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:43 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T03:49:38Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T03:49:40Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 03:44 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T03:49:41Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 2 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T03:49:41Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read the service register - the service calls io-pricing (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-summary-cache (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-pay (third-party, owned by IO Payments Ltd)
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T03:49:41Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 36 {T11.2} minutes 2 {T11.3} seconds before 03:49:02 {T11.4}
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T03:49:42Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 101 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T03:49:50Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Read what the deployment of 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72 changed
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T03:49:51Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T14.2} replicas run revision 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72, deployed at 03:42:44 {T14.3}

  - [T17] 2026-11-11T03:49:52Z {T17.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T17.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T17.3} hour before 03:49:51 {T17.4}
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T03:49:56Z {T18.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate

  - [T25] 2026-11-11T03:53:45Z {T25.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/551

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-10T23:42:44Z {P1.1} deploy 544cef36a8eaf45c5b030c3d5c21473d8176cef3 by kuki: deployed revision 544cef36a8eaf45c5b030c3d5c21473d8176cef3 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - [P2] 2026-11-11T03:42:44Z {P2.1} deploy 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72 by kuki: deployed revision 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - Flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 56 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 37 {G46bc.2} minutes, 03:13–03:49 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 33 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 37 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 03:13–03:49 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 2.50% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.00% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 03:26 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 4 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 22 {Gad41.2} minutes, 03:18–03:39 {Gad41.3}
  - [Gd3f7] ERROR io-shop: summary cache lookup failed - connection refused to redis://cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local:6380 (# of 200 {Gd3f7.1} requests) - 8 {Gd3f7.2} occurrences in 8 {Gd3f7.3} minutes, 03:42–03:49 {Gd3f7.4}; # was 50 {Gd3f7.5} to 200 {Gd3f7.6}, typically 200 {Gd3f7.7}, highest at 03:43 {Gd3f7.8}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] The deploy of revision 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72 at 2026-11-11T03:42:44Z {C1.1} changed cache.port in deploy/values-production.yaml from 6379 {C1.2} to 6380 {C1.3}. The summary cache refuses connections on 6380 {C1.4}, so cache_hit_ratio fell to 0 {C1.5} and p50 latency rose from about 26ms {C1.6} to about 190ms {C1.7}. The cache itself is healthy and the source code is unchanged. [config-induced-failure, confidence 0.93 {C1.8}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Rolled back the deployment of io-shop for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What each deployment it looked into changed:
  - [D1] Deployment of revision 0d8e826225f0de73958a8a8dd3d867b2ae249e72 to io-shop, compared against 544cef36a8eaf45c5b030c3d5c21473d8176cef3 - the revision deployed before it.
      modified deploy/values-production.yaml
        @@ -22,4 +22,4 @@ resources:
         # address is right.
         cache:
           host: cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local
        -  port: 6379 {D1.1}
        +  port: 6380 {D1.2}
  - A file [D1] does not list is as it was at the revision [D1] compares against.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] **What was wrong:** `deploy/values-production.yaml` sets `cache.port: 6380`. The investigation's evidence shows every summary cache lookup in production failing with "connection refused to redis://cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local:6380", and the investigation says the cache itself is healthy. 6379 {F1.1} was the port before the deploy and is the one the cache serves on. The wrong value is in this file.
      
      **The change:**
      - `deploy/values-production.yaml`: `cache.port` goes from 6380 {F1.2} back to 6379 {F1.3}. Nothing else in the file changes.
      - New test `tests/io_shop/test_deploy_values.py`: reads the production values file, finds the top-level `cache:` block by parsing lines (so it adds no YAML dependency), and checks that `port` is 6379 {F1.4} and `host` is `cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local`.
      
      **What the test is for:** The port check is written to fail against the file as it stands (6380 {F1.5}) and to pass with this change. Its job is to make a future change to the cache address show up in review and CI, not only as a fall in cache hit ratio after a deploy.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] deploy/values-production.yaml at 0d8e826
      # Deployment configuration for the io-shop account service, production.
      #
      # Rendered into the cluster as a ConfigMap and mounted into the pod, which is
      # why the service reads this file rather than being handed environment
      # variables: the values here are the deployment's, not the code's, and changing
      # one is a change to configuration that ships without the service being rebuilt.
      #
      # Owned by whoever runs the shop. Changes here go out the way any other change
      # goes out - reviewed, merged, and synced by the platform - and land without a
      # single line of io-shop's source being touched.
      
      replicas: 3 {S1.1}
      
      resources:
        memoryLimitMiB: 2048 {S1.2}
      
      # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
      #
      # The account page reads this cache before it works a shopper's spend figure
      # out, and recomputes when the cache has nothing or cannot be reached. So the
      # shop stays correct whatever is written here - it only stays *fast* while the
      # address is right.
      cache:
        host: cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local
        port: 6380 {S1.3}
      

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Rolled back the deployment of io-shop
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-3 (mitigate, open): Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand
PR #551 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The production values file had `cache.port` changed from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, and the summary cache refused connections on that port. Every summary-cache lookup failed, so on every request the account page fell back to working out each shopper's spend figure from scratch. That fallback keeps pages correct but slow.
cause_in_plain_words: A configuration change gave the shop a cache address that refused its connections, so every account page had to be worked out from scratch: the pages stayed correct but got slow.
still_at_risk: The refused cache port, or another wrong cache address, could reach production again and slow every account page.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly: the slowest replica's median time to answer a request rose far above its usual level, while failed requests stayed within their normal range. (cites AL1)
causal_chain 2: Pages were slow because the account page could not use its rendered-summary cache. Its configuration says that when the cache cannot be reached, the page works out the shopper's spend figure from scratch, and the logs show that happening on every request. (cites S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; Gd3f7, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: The cache could not be used because every lookup was refused: the service connected to the cache on port {S1.3}, and the cache refused the connection. As read at {T14.1}, all replicas ran revision 0d8e826, whose configuration sets that port. (cites Gd3f7, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; T14, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: The service pointed at that port because the deploy of revision 0d8e826 at {P2.1} changed the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, a port on which the cache refused connections. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed")
causal_chain 4 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 544cef3 at {P1.1}: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset at {began}. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4 ruled_out 3: A source-code change shipped in the same deploy: the diff lists only deploy/values-production.yaml, so every other file was as it was at the previous revision. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen, in review or before the deploy, that the cache address in the deployment configuration accepts connections. A change to the cache port shipped to production unchallenged.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The refused port would have been caught before the deploy, and no account page would have slowed.
contributing_factors 2: The deploy reached every replica, and no gate was seen that watches latency or cache-lookup failures after rollout to halt or reverse it.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The rollout would have stopped or reversed itself on the first replicas, before every shopper was served by the slow fallback.
contributing_factors 3: No alert on summary-cache lookup failures was seen. The fault was found only by the latency alert, although connection-refused errors were logged from the first minute.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on cache lookup failures would have pointed straight at the cache and could have fired sooner than a latency rule that waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding.
action_items 1: Add a pre-deploy check, in CI or at sync, that for every change to io-shop's deployment values confirms the configured cache host and port accept connections from the target environment, and blocks the deploy if they do not.
action_items 2: Roll io-shop deploys out progressively, with automated analysis that halts and rolls back the rollout when latency or summary-cache lookup failures rise on the first replicas.
action_items 3: Add an alert on io-shop summary-cache lookup failures (connection refused or unreachable).
action_items 4: Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the HighLatency alert on io-shop was linked to no on-call incident.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
